moments.title: Central banks own thousands of tons of gold bars
moments.summary: The speaker opens by defining a central bank as the bank that manages a country's money — the RBI in India — and points out that the RBI, the US and countries worldwide hold thousands of tons of actual gold bars, held as bars rather than as jewellery.
moments.evidence: Countries around the world own thousands of tons of gold, not jewelry, actual gold bars locked away in walls.

moments.title: Gold as a shock absorber when markets get bumpy
moments.summary: The explanation of why: when markets become uncertain, economies slow and currencies come under pressure, gold behaves differently from other assets — not the fastest or most exciting asset, but one that cushions the ride.
moments.evidence: gold often behaves differently from other assets. Think of it as a shock absorber.

moments.title: Gold pays no interest and no dividends, yet countries still own it
moments.summary: The closing argument: gold pays neither interest nor dividends, but countries still choose to hold it, because sometimes an asset's job is to protect you rather than to make you rich.
moments.evidence: Gold doesn't pay interest. It doesn't pay dividends. But yet countries around the world still choose to own it.
